The source notes that the sheng reached Europe in the eighteenth century and provided the theoretical basis for designing free-reed wind instruments; the earliest known prototype was made by Friedrich Buschmann of Berlin in 1821. Diatonic, chromatic, tremolo, octave, orchestral and bass types later developed, and the ten-hole diatonic type is often called the blues harp. The chromatic type adds a button slider and wind valves so that notes can be raised or lowered; in the mid twentieth century blues players also began to amplify the harmonica with a microphone and valve amplifier.

Its sound lies between the warmth of the woodwind and the sharpness of metal, warm yet still penetrating. Its range covers some three to four octaves, from low to high, and can carry many musical styles. Because it uses free reeds, resonance is shaped mainly by the space in the mouth, and the player can vary the embouchure and the strength of the airstream to produce a wealth of timbral change. Compared with the flute the harmonica is fuller and warmer; compared with the guitar it is more penetrating. Its multiple reeds give it the ability to play harmony, so that one instrument can produce a full sound, which suits blues, folk and rock in particular.

The harmonica is a free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 412.132. The player uses lips and tongue to direct the airstream into and out of the holes in the mouthpiece, setting the reeds in the air chambers vibrating; the basic parts are the comb, the reed plates and the cover plates. The common ten-hole diatonic type has ten air channels and twenty reeds, and there are also chromatic, tremolo, octave, horn, alto, bass and chord types. The harmonica is used in blues, American folk, classical, jazz, country and rock, and also for the bass or chord parts of harmonica ensembles.
